newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military must keep two-war force - Cohen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military must keep two-war force - Cohen.

text.p: The U.S. military must retain its current ability to win two regional wars at once despite the expense of foreign deployments and modern weapons, Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Monday.

He said the Quadrennial Defence Review, a new Pentagon assessment of U.S. strategy and power, had determined that "our forces must not fall short in their ability to respond to all types of threats" as the world's only remaining superpower.

"The QDR has determined that U.S. armed forces must be capable of fighting and winning two major theatre wars nearly simultaneously," he told officials of the private Brookings Institution think tank in a speech.
The review will be sent to Congress late this week and unveiled formally by Cohen and military leaders at the Pentagon next week.

The secretary declined to give other details of what the QDR will recommend to lawmakers except to reiterate that Washington will continue to keep 100,000 troops in Europe and 100,000 in the western Pacific for the forseeable future.

But defence officials have said privately that Cohen will recommend closing additional domestic military bases, cutting the 1.4 million-member U.S. armed forces by some 60,000 troops, cutting some warships and shrinking planned fighter jet programmes in order to save money for arms modernisation.

U.S. force structure has been driven in recent years by the ability to fight two major conflicts at once, possibly in the Middle Earces that are agile, flexible and responsive in a dynamic and uncertain world, forces that can quickly descend on and dominate any situation, and forces that can halt and defeat military aggression by major regional powers, even in two places across the globe," Cohen told the Brookings officials.
He reiterated warnings made last week that the Pentagon was preparing to make cuts in its civilian bureaucracy and would draw up a plan to cut even his own office before the year is out.

Cohen noted that some members of Congress were already complaining about any politically difficult decision to close more bases. Many communities rely on a nearby large U.S. military presence for their financial health.
"I heard the echoes of the signs from the road of the past: Don't close bases, don't cut troops, don't touch depots, don't even think about touching tac air (tactical aircraft programs)," Cohen said.
"We do know how we are not going to reach the future we want. It is not by taking the road well travelled -- that road is gone," he cautioned.
